docs.merging.component: MECHANICS — the rules a DESK plays by, as opposed to the gestures a hand makes on it.
The gesture shelf answers "what does the kit do when a finger does this". This one answers
"what does a desk do", and they are two shelves because they are not the same author: a
gesture is the kit's, and a rule about which pieces belong together is the game's. Every page
here is written in the catalog, on top of the same kit, through the same doors a game would use.
docs.merging.scene: STACK MERGING — the same finger and the same handles, and a heap that has an OPINION about what
goes into it.
Every stacking page before this one answers "are these one pile" with "do they touch". That is
the honest floor of the mechanic and it is not enough to deal a hand on: cards thrown across a
desk land where they land, and one that stops with a corner over two different deals joins both
of them — pick either up and it comes along, out of a hand it was never in.
So this desk asks three questions where the older ones asked one.
WHAT IT IS. A card heaps with a card, a chip only with a chip of its OWN denomination, a die
only with a die. The piece carries the answer itself (`Heaping`) rather than having it worked
out about it, so a fourth kind added tomorrow states its own pile instead of waiting for
somebody to remember a list.
HOW MUCH THEY MEET. An overlap, as a share of a piece's own area, against the number on the
panel. Turn it down to nothing and the old desk is back — which is the honest way to show what
the rule bought. It is measured the same way the tap ladder measures what shows, and it is
deliberately not the same number: a pile packed tightly enough to hide its lower cards would be
one that no card could ever be added to.
AND WHICH WAY UP THEY ARE LYING — unless the one that disagrees is the one you just put there.
A face-down deck dropped onto face-up cards does not swallow them; a face-up card dropped onto
a face-down pile joins it. Same two facings and the same overlap: what tells them apart is
which arrived last, and the desk already knows that, because the last thing put down is the
thing drawn on top. A mismatch is forgiven exactly once, at the top of the pile.
The desk opens with a closed deck, one card face up beside it, ten chips of each of three
denominations and two dice, and nothing touching anything.
